paragraphs: There's a generation of 30-year-olds in India with good jobs, quietly asking strangers online if they're finally allowed to spend on themselves.
Swipe to read →
I'm only half joking. Once the eldest starts earning, the bills just appear.
Papa's old loan from the village moneylender, at some crazy interest rate. Their own education loan too.
Then the younger one's college fees. Mummy's hospital bills. And eventually both parents' entire retirement.
Nobody sits them down and asks. It just starts around 23 and never officially stops.
Because nobody asked, there's no clear end. No last EMI. No "okay beta, you've done enough, go live your life."
So you get 29 and 30 year olds asking online if they're finally allowed to spend on themselves.
Grown adults with good jobs, asking for permission. That honestly tells you everything about how this works.
The family isn't evil here. That's what makes it so hard. They're genuinely grateful.
Every relative hears how much the eldest has done. But that praise is exactly what keeps the whole thing running.
You can't walk away from being the pillar of the family.
After a few years it stops being something you do. It becomes who you are. Buying yourself something nice starts to feel like stealing.
And nobody does the maths on what comes next.
The eldest spends their whole twenties paying for their parents' old age. Which means they're not saving for their own.
Late marriage. Late house. No real retirement fund of their own.
So by 60 they're exactly where their parents were. And guess who they'll need? Their own eldest kid.
It's basically a loan every generation takes from the next one.
The interest gets paid in someone's twenties. Everyone keeps saying India's young population is its biggest advantage.
But in millions of homes that dividend is already spent. Paid off quietly by someone nobody ever asked.

hook_candidates.hook: The most underrated financial product in India is the eldest child. No pension, no savings, no problem. And I know how that sounds.
There's a generation of 30-year-olds in India with good jobs, quietly asking strangers online if they're finally allowed to spend on themselves.
Picture a loan that starts the year you turn 23, has no last EMI, and nobody ever officially asked you to take it.
The eldest child doesn't keep paying for everyone because the family forces them. They keep paying because everyone keeps saying thank you.
Here's where India's eldest children end up. By 60, right where their parents were, needing their own kid to carry them.

paragraphs: I genuinely think the most underrated financial product in India is the eldest child.
No pension, no health insurance, no emergency fund? Doesn't matter. The family has a first-born who just got a job.

I'm only half joking. Look at what gets paid for in a lot of middle-class homes once the eldest starts earning:
– Papa's old loan from the village moneylender, at some crazy interest rate
– Their own education loan
– The younger one's college fees
– Mummy's hospital bills
– Eventually, both parents' entire retirement
Nobody sits them down and asks. It just starts around 23 and never officially stops.
And because nobody asked, there's no point where it ends. No last EMI. No "okay beta, you've done enough, go live your life."

So you get 29 and 30 year olds asking strangers online if they're finally allowed to spend money on themselves. Grown adults with good jobs, asking for permission. That honestly tells you everything about how this works.
The family isn't evil here, and that's what makes it so hard. They're genuinely grateful. Every relative hears about how much the eldest has done.
But that praise is exactly what keeps the whole thing running. You can't really walk away from a role where everyone calls you the pillar of the family.
After a few years it stops being something you do and becomes who you are. Buying yourself something nice starts to feel like stealing.
And the part nobody does the maths on is what happens 30 years later.
The eldest spends their twenties paying for their parents' old age, which means they're not saving for their own. Late marriage, late house, no real retirement fund.
So by 60 they're exactly where their parents were. And guess who they'll need? Their own eldest kid.
It's basically a loan every generation takes from the next one, and the interest gets paid in someone's twenties.
Everyone keeps saying India's young population is its biggest advantage. Demographic dividend and all that.
But in millions of homes that dividend is already spent. It's sitting in a hospital bill and a village loan, paid off quietly by someone nobody ever asked.
